## 1. Direct answer

The 0.1-second step sits in the model contract because in a fixed-step fluid model the
step is not a solver convenience; it is the declared resolution at which the model decides
how much can happen in one update. Every flow is computed per step, so the step scales
arrivals, admissions and completions, gives the per-step invariants their meaning, and
changes the metrics a decision would read. Left to the engine, the same model file could
produce different numbers under a different engine setting or engine version with no change
to the model, its hash, its validity claim or its review record; a reader could not see the
resolution choice without reading the engine; and nobody could challenge the assumption
before it shaped a decision. Declared in the contract, the step is visible, reviewable and
hash-bound, it invalidates stored runs when it changes, and it fails replay exactly as a
changed input should.

A coarse step can manufacture behaviour because the discretisation is itself a mechanism. A
whole interval of arrivals is offered at once, so admission and rejection happen in
step-sized bursts; once one step's service capacity exceeds the admission buffer, the queue
is emptied every step and the reported rejection rate and throughput become properties of
the step rather than of the modelled system; and an unguarded update can serve more work
than exists, producing negative stock or overshoot. The volume names the reporting failure
exactly: "A coarse step produces overshoot or negative stock, and the analyst reports the
artifact as behavior" (What the model fails section of the stock-and-flow page).

## 3. Mechanism and justification: why the step is a declared model input

**3.1 The step scales every flow, so it is part of the equations.** The stock-and-flow
update is written per interval: the change in backlog over a small interval is the
difference between the two flows, and every flow term is a rate multiplied by the step.
At 30 requests per second, a 0.1-second step offers 3 requests and a 10-second step offers
300; service is correspondingly capped at service rate times the step. Changing the step
therefore changes admitted, served and rejected amounts before any engine question arises.
The contract lists dynamics as "model family, equations and integration step", so the step
is filed with the equations, not with the executor.

**3.2 The step is the numeric form of the declared abstraction.** The contract requires an
abstraction block covering "time unit, state unit, boundary and resolution", and the
order-intake model states its resolution as fixed-step fluid integration in which
individual requests are not represented. The step is what that sentence means in numbers:
it says what the model can and cannot resolve. A resolution that exists only as an engine
default is an abstraction claim the reader cannot inspect, which defeats the stated purpose
of the contract: a reader should be able to see state, units, assumptions and verification
evidence "without reading the engine". The contract exists because a diagram, or an engine
setting, can leave every decision hidden; a contract "forces those choices into named
fields that a validator can check and a reader can challenge".

**3.3 The invariants are per-step, so the step defines what they test.** Conservation and
non-negativity are asserted at every step and after every update, and the model refuses a
negative backlog. A per-step invariant is only meaningful relative to a step: at 10 seconds
the check tests a different update than at 0.1 seconds. Declaring the step makes the scope
of the invariant explicit instead of inheriting it from whatever the engine happened to do.

**3.4 Declaring it is the only way to bind the number to the provenance chain.** A run
record binds the run to the model and scenario hashes, an input hash over model, scenario
and engine version, and a result hash; the model and scenario files are the canonical
inputs, and a change to either invalidates the run until it is regenerated. If the step
lived in the engine, a step change would be either invisible (a runtime setting that no
hash covers) or an engine version bump in which an execution detail stands in for a
modelling assumption, with no edit to the model hash and no update to the model's validity
claim. Declared in the model, a step change moves the model hash, invalidates stored runs
and fails replay, which is the correct behaviour for a changed assumption.

**3.5 It keeps the engine substitutable and the assumption owned by the model.** The
engine's scope rule is that a model family needing a new mechanism "gets a new explicit
contract, not an unrecorded engine extension". A step chosen inside the engine is such an
extension: it lets the executor refine or coarsen the model without a contract change, so
two engines, or two versions of one engine, could disagree about the same model file and
neither would be wrong by its own lights.

**3.6 Declaration buys reviewability, not adequacy.** The validator checks the schema, the
identifier, scenario references and parameter evidence; it "cannot check that a source
actually supports a parameter", and it certainly cannot judge whether 0.1 seconds is fine
enough. Declaring the step converts an invisible default into a claim that a person can
challenge, with a resolution sentence and a validity limit next to it.

## 4. How a coarse step produces behaviour that is only an artefact

**4.1 Batched admission.** Offerings arrive as one lump per step. Admission is the minimum
of the offered lump and the room left in the buffer, so at a coarse step the buffer is
tested once per interval rather than continuously. Rejection therefore happens in
step-sized bursts at step boundaries, and peak backlog and time-to-drain are quantised.

**4.2 Over-service, negative stock and overshoot.** The volume states the mechanism: "A
large step can admit a whole interval of arrivals at once, serve more than the available
backlog, and produce a negative stock." The shipped order-intake model caps service at
available work, so it cannot literally go negative; but the cap converts the arithmetic
error into a different artefact: service per step becomes the step's capacity rather than
the system's work, and any feedback path acquires a synthetic one-step delay, which is
enough to create overshoot or oscillation that no part of the modelled system contains. The
volume notes separately that a real delay can produce oscillation "even when every
individual decision is locally reasonable"; a step adds a delay the model never declared.

**4.3 A hand trace of the declared rule, using the documented saturation workload.** The
documented saturation case is 30 requests per second offered against 24 per second of
service capacity with an admission bound of 80 requests over a 3,600-second horizon after
a 300-second warmup. Applying the declared update rule (offered equals arrival rate times
step; admitted equals the minimum of offered and remaining room; served equals the minimum
of available work and service rate times step) gives:

| Step (s) | Rejection rate | Throughput (req/s) | Mean backlog (req) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.01 | 0.200 | 24.0 | 79.8 |
| 0.1 | 0.200 | 24.0 | 77.6 |
| 1 | 0.200 | 24.0 | 56.0 |
| 5 | 0.467 | 16.0 | 0.0 |
| 10 | 0.733 | 8.0 | 0.0 |

This is my arithmetic on the documented equations and the documented workload, not a
recorded V12 run; the 0.1 row reproduces the published 77.6-request backlog, which is
itself the capacity minus service rate times the step (80 minus 2.4). The table shows two
distinct artefact regimes. Below the buffer's drain time (capacity divided by service
capacity, about 3.3 seconds) rejection and throughput are stable but the reported mean
backlog is literally a function of the step: 77.6 requests at 0.1 seconds against 56 at
1 second, a 28 per cent difference in a metric a decision record could read. Above that
threshold one step can serve the entire buffer, so the queue empties every step and the
reported rejection rate and throughput become properties of the step, not of the system:
0.2 rejection and 24 requests per second at 0.1 seconds against 0.73 and 8 at 10 seconds.
An analyst who reported either row as intake behaviour would be reporting the
discretisation.

**4.4 Conservation does not detect it.** In the trace above, offered requests equal
completed plus rejected plus backlog to floating-point tolerance in every row. The
per-step identity, the non-negativity assertion and a deterministic replay all pass at a
coarse step, because they test the implemented arithmetic, not the adequacy of the
resolution. The verification matrix covers conservation, boundary cases, event ordering,
timeouts, retries and replay; it contains no step-refinement case, and the page listing
what is not verified names calibration and operational validity but not resolution. This
is the precise sense in which the behaviour is "only an artefact": it is reproducible,
invariant-preserving, hash-stable and wrong. Reproducibility is not validity. The same
class of error is documented for another modelling choice: a model with an unbounded queue
"never rejects; it accumulates backlog and reports a latency that is an artifact of the
horizon". A step-selected rejection burst is the same error with a clock instead of a
horizon.

## 5. Boundaries and trade-offs

- **Declared is not adequate.** The contract fixes the value and exposes it; nothing in
  V12 tests that 0.1 seconds is fine enough, and no recorded run compares step sizes. The
  defensible statement is "declared, fixed and challengeable", not "validated".
- **Finer is not automatically truer.** A discrete-event model "is not automatically more
  accurate; it can be wrong at a finer resolution", and a very small step costs runtime and
  can create false precision. The fluid model still ignores individual latency, retries
  and timeout ordering, as its validity limits say.
- **The engine must honour the declaration.** The shipped engine reads the step from the
  model parameters and falls back to a default when the value is absent (repository
  inspection of the engine module, not a book claim). That fallback is exactly the private
  default the contract removes for this model; the required schema field is what keeps the
  declaration from being decorative.
- **Null is a legitimate value.** The event-driven checkout model declares a null step
  because time advances from event to event. The field must be present so that "not
  applicable" is distinguishable from "unstated"; the order-intake model is the case where
  a numeric step is mandatory in practice.
- **The step matters only through decision-relevant metrics.** The scope checklist asks
  whether added detail "can change a metric that can reverse the decision". If peak
  backlog, rejection or throughput can reverse a comparison, the step is decision-relevant
  and deserves a refinement or sensitivity check; if not, a coarse step is a documented
  cost saving rather than a defect.
- **The step is not a calibration claim.** Every V12 input is assumed, the model is
  uncalibrated, and its validity is limited to a synthetic workload. A well-chosen step
  makes the fluid approximation numerically stable; it says nothing about a real intake
  system.
- **A small step is not a substitute for structure.** It cannot recover individual request
  latency, retry amplification or timeout ordering that the model family does not contain,
  and it does not repair an omitted boundary.

## 7. Unknowns and confidence

- **No step-refinement evidence exists in the accessed pages.** No recorded run compares
  0.1 seconds with a finer or coarser step, and the verification matrix has no such case.
  The adequacy of 0.1 seconds is therefore asserted, declared and reviewable, not
  demonstrated. A refinement run showing decision-relevant metrics stable across steps
  would strengthen it; one showing drift would weaken the published saturation numbers.
- **No selection rule is given.** The sources describe the trade-off (large step, arithmetic
  failure; small step, runtime cost) but do not state a rule such as a maximum step relative
  to the smallest time constant or the buffer drain time. The threshold in section 4.3 is my
  derivation from the equations.
- **The shipped guard changes the failure mode.** Because service is capped at available
  work, literal negative stock is prevented in the implemented model; the residual risks are
  batched admission, resolution floors and any feedback added later. The volume's negative
  stock example describes the unguarded form.
- **Confidence.** High on why the step is declared (direct statements, schema requirements,
  hash and replay rules, and the equations). High on the artefact mechanism for batched
  admission and step-dependent reported metrics (derived arithmetically and consistent with
  the published 77.6 figure). Medium on the wider taxonomy (overshoot, oscillation,
  quantised latency): those follow from the fixed-step update and the feedback discussion,
  but the volume does not run that experiment.
- **Not established here.** That any real intake system behaves like any step size; that the
  model is calibrated; that the decision records are accepted; that independent review or CI
  occurred.

## 8. Search and saturation notes

Describe was run first; the question needs the modeling-and-simulation layer (models,
contracts, verification, limits) and limited book-layer support for the stock/flow and
resolution vocabulary. Fourteen search calls used several formulations per facet (exact
terms, synonyms, layer aliases, conceptual queries) with volume modeling-and-simulation and
book; search has no offset and responses were truncated by the character budget, so I
refined queries and read each cited page in full with page/read, paginating where needed.
The last two search rounds returned only sections already read plus unrelated pages, so I
took the facet space as saturated. Repository artifacts (model JSON, schema, engine module)
were inspected for context only; they are not cited as section evidence. No file was
edited, no run was recorded and no commit was made.
